Clause (a) 'first-party standard library' is satisfied only by modules the language's own official documentation presents as part of that language's standard library or core libraries AND that are importable under the frozen build recipe with no dependency declaration and no additional install. This is the single rule that keeps C++ and Swift comparable on this host.

Where an index publishes an entry-update date rather than an upstream release date (vcpkg), the index entry's own publication date in the official index repository was used, recorded as such. Not 20: that band requires N <= 3 and six standard-library modules were located in the toolchain under test and confirmed by reading the shipped source and its official doc comments. Zig has a package manager but no package index: `zig fetch` takes a URL, a git server or a tarball, and neither ziglang.org's documentation nor its learn pages name a registry, index or default remote, so no index satisfies any of the three index_selection_rule qualification clauses and only standard-library coverage can satisfy a domain. cross_language_consistency_note: The same level means the same thing for all ten because the level is a pure function of N, and N was produced by one identical procedure. (1) The same twelve frozen domains and the same twelve frozen query strings were issued, verbatim, in the same B01..B12 order, exactly once per domain per language, for all ten; no synonym, retry or language-specific string was used anywhere. (2) The same two-step order was applied everywhere: the shipped standard library first, the single qualifying package index second. (3) The same clause-(a) definition of 'standard library' was applied to all ten - modules the language's own official documentation presents as its standard or core library AND importable under the frozen build recipe with no dependency declaration - which is what keeps C++ and Swift comparable on a macOS host, since it excludes macOS SDK C libraries from C++ and Apple platform frameworks (CoreML, Accelerate, Metal, CryptoKit, os.Logger, Compression) from Swift alike. (4) The same 24-month window, ending at the 2026-09-17 cutoff, was applied to every index result, and results published after the cutoff were excluded for every language (this excluded one npm package for TypeScript). (5) The same three domain-reading decisions were fixed before scoring and applied to all ten: cloud-service SDK clients do not satisfy B05 (this cost Go, Java and Kotlin their top default-ordered results), parsers/formatters/query-builders do not satisfy B01 or B03 (this cost C++, Rust, TypeScript, Java and Kotlin their top results), and B10 is read as the logging domain its frozen provenance mapping names rather than requiring the literal word 'structured' (which is what lets Zig's std.log count, and would not have changed any other language's N). (6) The re-read across the ten assignments confirms the two required invariants. No two languages with the same observable evidence got different levels: Java and Kotlin were searched in the same index with the same strings, the same single domain (B09) failed for both, and both are 11/80; Zig and Quidra both have a standard library and no qualifying package index, both cover exactly six domains, and both are 6/40; Python, Rust, Go, TypeScript and Swift each cover all twelve and are all 100. No two languages with clearly different evidence got the same level: C++, Java and Kotlin sit at 11 while the five 12s sit above them, and the separation in every case is a domain that is genuinely uncovered under the frozen procedure and is named, with its rejected candidates and their dates, in that language's record. (7) Quidra was examined last, after all nine other records were written, and nothing about the procedure was decided or revised after seeing it.

Two index entries dated after the cutoff were found and explicitly excluded (@fynjs/cli-args 1.1.3, npm, 2026-09-18 for TypeScript B09; software.amazon.awssdk:machinelearning 2.55.0, Maven Central, 2026-09-17 was in-window but rejected on other grounds). All other recorded artifacts predate the cutoff. Index result ORDERINGS, however, were observed one day after the cutoff and may differ marginally from an ordering observed on 2026-09-17; this affects all ten languages identically.

B09 for C++, Java and Kotlin is the single most consequential finding and an auditor must understand its cause. It is not a claim that those ecosystems lack command-line argument parsers - they plainly contain picocli, CLI11, clipp, clap-like libraries and many others. It is the mechanical result of frozen_query_list: the frozen string is the full phrase 'command line argument parsing', frozen_query_list.no_second_query forbids any retry, and Maven Central's own default search returns literally zero results for that phrase while vcpkg's returns exactly one package whose most recent publication of any kind (2024-07-16 index entry, 2023-08-08 upstream release) falls outside the 24-month window. The same phrase DOES return qualifying results on crates.io, npm, the Swift Package Index and PyPI, and Python, Go, TypeScript and Quidra satisfy B09 from their standard libraries. Scored strictly as written, this costs C++, Java and Kotlin 20 points each. Nothing in the frozen document permits rephrasing the query at scoring time.

Zig B08 rests on one judgement: std.gpu ships SPIR-V shader built-ins but no renderer or GUI, and was scored as not covering 'Graphical user interface or 2D/3D graphics rendering'. Reading it the other way would make Zig N=7 and move it from 40 to 60. The reading applied is that a domain is covered by a library that performs the named capability, which is the same reading that rejected format parsers for B01/B03 in five other languages.

vcpkg (C++) does not publish per-package release dates on vcpkg.io, so the in-window date recorded for every C++ package is the last publication date of that port's entry in the official microsoft/vcpkg repository, obtained from the GitHub commits API and labelled as such. Every other index publishes a release or version date directly. The C++ verdict does not depend on this substitution: the one decisive package (arg-router) is out of window under both its index-entry date and its upstream release date.

The Swift Package Index search page displays repository activity recency ('Active N ago') rather than release dates, so for Swift the activity recency shown in the search result is recorded, and the package pages were opened to obtain explicit 'Latest Release / Released N ago' dates for the two packages where recency was near the window edge or where release existence was in doubt (simd-tools 0.0.4, swift-argument-parser 1.8.2; Numerix was rejected for having no published release at all). Exact calendar release dates for the remaining Swift packages could not be obtained because the GitHub releases API rate-limited this host during collection; all of them showed activity within days or weeks, far inside the window.

GitHub API rate limiting also prevented independent upstream release-date confirmation for the Swift selections listed above. No other language depended on that API except C++, whose port-date queries completed before the limit was reached.

Maven Central's browse API (POST /api/internal/browse/components) was used for the twelve Java/Kotlin queries because search.maven.org's Solr endpoint returned empty responses from this host; the zero-result verdict for B09 was independently confirmed in Maven Central's own web UI, which reported 'Showing 0 results out of the 884469 available packages' with its default 'Best Match' ordering.

PyPI's search endpoint returns a bot-challenge page to curl from this host, so Python's four index queries were issued through the desktop app's browser pane against the same pypi.org/search URLs with PyPI's default relevance ordering. The rendered page was in Japanese (the browser profile's locale); dates are recorded in the ISO form of the displayed Japanese dates.

Java's index qualification rests on clause (ii) rather than a direct reference: no page inside Java's frozen official_docs_root (openjdk.org, docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/) was found to name Maven Central. The chain used is that the JDK 26 Documentation Home at docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/ links 'Java Tutorials' to Oracle's dev.java, which names Maven as the build tool, and Apache Maven's own documentation states 'By default, Maven will download from the central repository.' An auditor who rejects that chain would leave Java with no qualifying index, dropping it to standard-library-only coverage of 8 domains and a score of 60. Kotlin is unaffected: kotlinlang.org names mavenCentral() directly.

For Quidra, no capability was scored from documentation alone: every one of the twelve domains was probed by executing `quidra check` on a source file on this host, and both the six passes and the five named absence failures (sql, crypto, gui, log, compress) are recorded with their compiler diagnostics.
